stance_basis: opens letter calling EO 11644 an unconstitutional revocation of rights and demanding its rescission
summary: R. H. Schif, a Glenwood Springs, CO resident, wrote to Senator Floyd Haskell expressing strong opposition to Executive Order 11644, which he viewed as an unconstitutional infringement on public land access rights for off-road vehicle users. He argued the order created 'puppet dictators' among land administrators, discriminated against millions of four-wheel drive vehicle users, harmed Colorado's hunting and fishing economy, and should be rescinded before any further wilderness designations are considered.
complaint_summary: R. H. Schif writes to Senator Haskell opposing EO 11644, arguing it unconstitutionally restricts public land access, creates authoritarian land administrators, discriminates against millions of four-wheel drive users, damages Colorado's hunting/fishing economy, and should be rescinded.

statement.text:
This correspondence is for the purpose of registering my indignation and opposition concerning the implementation of Executive Order 11644. This order is apparently the result of pressures from various hysterical groups such as the Sierra Club and the hippies, if there's a difference.
Following are a few reasons which I feel justify my attitude toward the subject.
Contrary to the opening wording of the order, I feel that indirectly it says that, "By virtue of the power vested in me as President of the United States, I hereby revoke your constitutional right to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness."
The immediate result of this order has been to create a profusion of puppet dictators in the guise of land administrators.
Here in Colorado West, the authoritative agencies have installed large signs advising one to restrict travel to constructed roads only, under threat of monetary and penal consequences. They then post many constructed roads "off limits."
It can be assumed that this regulation has been imposed as a result of erroneous reports of excessive terrain or ecological damage. In my opinion, the majority of the complainants probably can't even define the word "ecology." Regrettably, you are probably not in a position to see and establish the truth in fact for yourself.
I have no quarrel with skiers or skiing and cannot speak for the rest of the country; however, I sincerely believe that the claimed vehicular damage in Colorado West, if laid end to end, would not equal the 27 miles by 60 feet of timber and vegetation eliminated for ski trails on public lands involved in just one small complex near here.
Statistically, there are roughly We to 5 million skiers and approximately 5 million four-wheel drive vehicles averaging three occupants each. This obviously affects 15 million public land users in contrast and indicates recreational group discrimination.

Colorado derives income each year of 5 to 7 million dollars from the sale of hunting and fishing licenses alone. I predict that this income will be effectively reduced by 85 percent within two years as a result of this order.
Location and development of much needed new mineral and petroleum resources are severely handicapped accordingly.
There are many all-terrain vehicles available which, because of their construction, virtually eliminate the possibility of terrain damage. The ground contact P.S.I. being 1/350 that of a horse. These apparently were not taken into consideration with the issuance of this order.
This literally forces off-road enthusiasts to streets and high-ways and probably will be reflected by a proportionate percentage increase in accident and fatality statistics.
The aged and infirm are pretty much left out of public land participation as a result.
There are many of us who, because of damages sustained in the battle against dictatorial oppression during World War II, do not go along with the aura surrounding this subject.
I personally believe that decisions such as these should be returned to the authority where they rightfully belong: The United States Congress.
Last year, Gordon Allott sent tapes to the regional radio stations proclaiming the Flat Tops area as a natural for inclusion into the wilderness because it was devoid of human development. In reality, the area has many rouds, etc., constructed under the authority of the Forest Service for the purpose of harvesting beetle-killed timber resulting from excessive predator control. This could have been a contributing factor in Allott's defeat because we are really not that stupid.
In no way do I feel that consideration should be extended for further land addition to the wilderness concept until Executive Order 11644 is rescinded.
Very truly yours,
R. H. Schif
